# Upcoming SaladCloud Price Changes: November 1, 2026

SaladCloud GPU pricing is changing on November 1, 2026: High, Medium, and Low Priority prices rise on 21 GPU classes. Lowest Priority is unchanged.

Jared Carpenter

Product Update SaladCloud Mon Oct 26 2026

We're raising GPU prices on SaladCloud where demand has outpaced supply. High, Medium, and Low Priority prices are going up on 21 GPU classes. Lowest Priority pricing is unchanged on every class.

These changes take effect Sunday, November 1, 2026 at 00:00 UTC, and they will impact active and running instances at that time.

## Summary Copy Anchor Link

- High Priority prices are increasing on 21 GPU classes, by 10% to 20% on most of them.
- Medium and Low Priority prices are increasing on the same 21 classes, by smaller amounts.
- Lowest Priority pricing is unchanged on every GPU class.
- Every GPU class not listed below is unchanged at every priority level.

## Why prices are going up Copy Anchor Link

Over the past several weeks, demand has outpaced supply on many of our most popular GPUs. Several classes have been running almost entirely at High Priority, and many of you have waited for capacity or not gotten it at all.

SaladCloud runs on GPUs that individuals share with the network, and those providers have other options. Paying them a competitive rate is how we keep the machines we have and bring new ones online, so alongside these price changes we're raising provider payouts to attract more supply.

The increases are also weighted toward High Priority. When nearly everything runs at High, priority stops meaning much. High rises the most, Medium and Low rise less, and Lowest stays the same, so the gap between tiers widens: High stays available for work that needs it, and the lower tiers have more room.

# Lambda announces GPU price rises of about 15% — B200, H100 and A100 80GB, from Nov 16

Nov 6, 2026

Read on Lambda's own pricing page today, Nov 6, 2026: the Instances table now prints the prices that take effect on Nov 16, 2026 — HGX B200 up $1.00 an hour, H100 up $0.60 and A100 80GB up $0.40. It is the largest single announced rise we have caught this autumn, and renters have ten days' notice.

Image: GPUJournal price record — read on lambda.ai/pricing

What was announced, in the pricing page's own words (read Nov 6, 2026): 'These prices take effect November 16, 2026, at 00:00 UTC. Until then, log in to your Lambda Cloud account to see current pricing.' The printed Nov 16 rates: HGX B200 $7.69 an hour (from the $6.69 last verified on Nov 5, +14.9%), HGX H100 $4.59 (from $3.99, +15.0%), HGX A100 80GB $3.19 (from $2.79, +14.3%), and HGX A100 40GB unchanged at $1.99. Lambda is also now at a new address — lambda.com — announced on its blog on Nov 5, 2026; the pricing page itself still answers at lambda.ai/pricing.

How we are treating it: an announced rise is not a live price. Our board keeps Lambda's last verified rates until Nov 16 and will move only when the new rates are re-verified in effect on or after that date — the rise is recorded in Price Watch today as announced, with both dates. One consequence of the announcement is already live, though: Lambda's currently-effective rates can no longer be read on its public page, only after logging in, so today's public check could verify the future rates but not re-read the current ones.

What it does to the board when it lands: Lambda's B200 at $6.69 is currently the cheapest verified HGX B200 instance rate we list from a self-serve cloud; at $7.69 it would sit above RunPod Community's $5.98 marketplace rate and just below RunPod Secure's $7.99. Its H100 at $4.59 would remain above the board's best H100 SXM offer (TensorDock, from $2.25 at an 8-GPU minimum) but move Lambda from the middle of the H100 pack toward its top. Around-the-clock, the announced rises add about $730 a month per B200, $438 per H100 and $292 per A100 80GB on a 730-hour month.

### What it means if you rent GPUs

Until today, this autumn's rises were either quiet list adjustments caught after the fact (Verda's ten) or rises read on the day they landed. Lambda has done the renter-friendly thing — announced, dated and quantified, ten days ahead — and the size is the story: about 15% at once, on the three cards that anchor most training budgets. Anyone renewing or reserving Lambda capacity this month now has a hard date to plan around, and Nov 16 becomes a date this desk will verify first thing.

results.title: Nebius raises GPU list prices up to 21% while H100 spot sits at $0.79 - CTOL Digital Solutions
highlights:
October 22, 2026

By

...

- What the live spot market shows
- Benchmarks for a GPU rental contract

Posted prices for four Nebius GPU types rose 17 to 21 percent on 1 October. Its own spot board shows Blackwell chips near 60 percent of list and an H100 at the floor, so the squeeze sits in particular chips and regions.

Nebius told CNBC this week that AI computing prices are rising faster than it expected. On 1 October it lifted the posted price of four GPU types by 17 to 21 percent. Anyone renting GPUs has to decide whether that posted price is what they will pay.

...

### What changed in the price list

The Nebius pricing documentation dates two changes. The first took effect on 1 October, when on demand prices per GPU hour rose for four chips. Reuters reported on 17 September that Nebius had announced it, its second price rise in three months.

- B300 went from $7.85 to $9.50, up 21.0 percent, the largest rise.
- B200 went from $7.15 to $8.50, up 18.9 percent.
- H200 went from $4.50 to $5.40, up 20.0 percent.
- H100 went from $3.85 to $4.50, up 16.9 percent, the smallest rise of the four.

The RTX PRO 6000 stayed at $1.80, so the rise did not reach every GPU.

The second change came on 8 October. The preemptible tier, which rents interruptible capacity at a discount, stopped using fixed prices. It moved to dynamic spot pricing that can change every 15 minutes.

One rule in the documentation matters most. The highest spot price is always one cent below the current on demand rate, so the new list price is a ceiling. The floor is $0.79 or $0.99 depending on the chip. The posted price rise matters to a spot buyer only when the market pushes against that ceiling.

results.title: Verda raises prices again — all nine GPUs up about 1%, the eighth rise since Oct 23 | GPUJournal
highlights:
# Verda raises prices again — all nine GPUs up about 1%, the eighth rise since Oct 23

Nov 2, 2026

Read on Verda's own pricing page today, Nov 2, 2026, against the figures read there on Nov 1: every GPU in Verda's range rose by about 1% — GB300, B300, B200, H200, H100, both A100s, the RTX PRO 6000 and the L40S. After two flat checks, the October rise run has resumed.

Image: Verda via verda.com

What changed, read on verda.com/pricing on Nov 2, 2026 (unrounded page figures in brackets): GB300 $13.05 → $13.18 [$13.18], B300 $11.35 → $11.46 [$11.46], B200 $8.87 → $8.96 [$8.958], H200 $6.25 → $6.31 [$6.313], H100 SXM $4.79 → $4.84 [$4.841], A100 80GB $2.25 → $2.27 [$2.270], A100 40GB $1.61 → $1.63 [$1.625], RTX PRO 6000 $2.65 → $2.67 [$2.671] and L40S $1.90 → $1.92 [$1.920]. Each move is within a cent of +1.0% — a uniform list adjustment, not one card repricing.

The pattern: Verda rose on Oct 23, 24, 26, 27, 28, 29 and 30, then held on Oct 31 and Nov 1 — and has now risen an eighth time. Its GB300, the only GB300 rate we list, has gone from $11.82 an hour at our Oct 19 check to $13.18 today, up 11.5% in two weeks. Verda is not alone in the pattern: Nebius raised across the board on Oct 1, RunPod Secure on Oct 14, and SaladCloud's 21-class Priority rise took effect on Nov 1, with SaladCloud saying demand had outpaced supply. Rising list prices are consistent with growing demand (our reading, labelled as interpretation; capacity and cost moves can produce the same shape).

What it costs: Verda holds the board's Best offer on only two cards — the GB300 and the A100 40GB — and both rose today, so those two best offers rose with it. Everywhere else the cheapest verified offers are other providers' and none moved: the board's H100 SXM best is still TensorDock at $2.25 an hour (at an 8-GPU minimum) and its B200 best is still RunPod Community at $5.98. If you rent at Verda around the clock, today's rise adds about $95 a month per GB300, $65 per B200 and $35 per H100 on a 730-hour month — small per hour, real per fleet.

Checked today and unchanged: RunPod Secure, Lambda, Nebius, CoreWeave, Thunder Compute and TensorDock all held at the rates read on Nov 1, and SaladCloud's new Priority rates (RTX 5090 High $0.60, RTX 4090 High $0.44) are still the live ones. Not checked today, and named rather than covered by the stamp: RunPod Community (its tier could not be separated in today's read), Hyperstack (its pricing table could not be read) and nafnaf.ai (its homepage showed no GPUs available today, so there was no live listing to verify).

### One Big Thing · Phase 3 · Compute

What happened: Nebius raised on-demand GPU prices on October 1, its second hike in about three months. Independent trackers show the same direction across the market.

Why it matters: The bear case on AI infrastructure assumed GPUs lose value fast. Rental rates are the cleanest test of that assumption, and so far the test is failing.

By the numbers:

- Nebius list price for an H100 went from $3.85 to $4.50 per GPU-hour; B300 from $7.85 to $9.50.
- The Ornn H100 index settled at $3.17 on October 23, up about 4% in a month.

# AWS is raising GPU instance prices by ~20% on July 1 — and quietly keeping its own Trainium chips at

Paul Nugent

Nov 4, 2026

AWS is raising GPU instance prices by ~20% on July 1 — and quietly keeping its own Trainium chips at the same price.

This is the most important AI infrastructure pricing story of the year, and the signal is unmistakable.

The move: ~20% price increase on EC2 Capacity Block reservations for Nvidia GPU instances, effective July 1. AWS cited "supply and demand dynamics" — meaning the global compute crunch has gotten severe enough that AWS believes customers will pay more without leaving.

The critical detail: Trainium pricing is unchanged.

AWS now operates two parallel compute economics tracks:

🔹 NVIDIA TRACK: +20% — you absorb Nvidia's pricing power, supply constraints, AND AWS's margin protection layered on top.

🔹 TRAINIUM TRACK: flat — Amazon subsidizes the economics because every workload that migrates to Trainium deepens lock-in to the AWS ecosystem.

results.title: GPU prices are rising for a reason that has nothing to do with GPUs. | Compute Stacker
results.author: Compute Stacker
highlights:
- All three merchant DRAM suppliers, Samsung, SK hynix and Micron, describe their 2026 HBM output as effectively committed or sold out
- TrendForce reports server DRAM contract prices rising quarter over quarter, citing supply shortages, low inventory and HBM crowding-out effects
- Dell'Oro estimates that if DRAM prices had held near pre-increase levels, cumulative server spending through 2030 would be roughly 10% lower, with the effect most pronounced in 2026 and 2027

What's reported but not confirmed: NVIDIA raising AI server system prices by around 15 to 17%. That comes from press reporting, not from NVIDIA.

The visible end of this is rate cards. Nebius raised H100 on-demand 16.9% and B300 21% on October 1, its second increase in three months. AWS raised reserved Capacity Block rates on October 7.

What it means for planning:

- Treat current list prices as a snapshot, not a trend line. Two major providers repriced within a week this month.
- If you're negotiating a commitment, the component cost environment is an argument both ways. Ask what happens if memory prices fall.
- Spot and preemptible tiers absorb this differently from committed contracts. Nebius's October 1 increase didn't touch committed contracts.
- Check your provider's rate card before you budget, not after.

results.title: GPU Rental Rates Rise on Solid AI Demand; Supply-Demand Imbalance Persists | StockHub
highlights:
## AI Summary

• Amazon stated that most of its 2027 supply and a significant portion of its 2028 supply are fully booked, while SpaceX also explained that compute rental requests exceed current supply. • In October, Nebius raised on-demand prices for major GPUs by approximately +17% to +21%, notably increasing the hourly rate for the B300 from $7.85 to $9.50. • Spot Preemptible VM prices are also priced without significant discounts compared to on-demand rates, reflecting strong GPU rental demand. • It is analyzed that short-term contracts allow GPU investment costs to be recouped with one year of revenue, and that resolving the supply-demand imbalance in the short term will be difficult due to the scarcity of immediately available compute.
